claim: Nine stable transgenic zebrafish lines were generated for targeted opsin expression using the GAL4/UAS binary expression system.
source: We generated nine stable UAS lines for opsins having different ion selectivities and spectral tuning, fused to a fluorescent protein reporter (tdTomato or eYFP; Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1; Asakawa et al., 2008; Arrenberg et al., 2009; Horstick et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the generation of nine stable transgenic lines and references Figure 1A showing the list of opsins.

claim: CoChR elicited escape responses in embryos at the highest response probability (65–100% at 112–445 μW/mm2) with blue light.
source: With blue light, CoChR elicited escapes at the highest response probability (65–100% at 112–445 μW/mm2; Figure 2F,G)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on response probability at defined irradiance levels, supported by Figure 2F,G.

claim: ChrimsonR was the only cation channelrhodopsin to evoke escapes using amber light (~70% response probability at 322 μW/mm2).
source: As expected from its red-shifted absorption spectrum, ChrimsonR was the only cation channelrhodopsin to evoke escapes using amber light (~70% response probability at 322 μW/mm2; Figure 2F,G; Klapoetke et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on ChrimsonR's response to amber light, supported by Figure 2F,G and a citation to prior work.

claim: GtACR1 triggered escapes upon amber and blue light stimulation whereas GtACR2 elicited responses only with blue light.
source: Consistent with their respective red- and blue-shifted absorption spectra, GtACR1 triggered escapes upon amber and blue light stimulation whereas GtACR2 elicited responses only with blue light (Figure 2F,G; Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the differential spectral responses of GtACR1 and GtACR2, supported by Figure 2F,G and a citation.

claim: CoChR elicited tail movements with the highest probability and shortest latency in response to blue light (96–100% at 0.63–2.55 mW/mm2).
source: Response probability increased with irradiance (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and CoChR again elicited tail movements with the highest probability and shortest latency in response to blue light (96–100% at 0.63–2.55 mW/mm2; Figure 3F,G).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on CoChR's efficacy in larval activation assays, supported by Figure 3F,G.

claim: Only the ChrimsonR line responded to red light (~78% response probability at 1 mW/mm2) in larval activation assays.
source: Only the ChrimsonR line responded to red light (~78% response probability at 1 mW/mm2; Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on ChrimsonR's response to red light in larvae, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: CoChR and ChrimsonR generated the largest photocurrents (CoChR 475 ± 186 pA, ChrimsonR 251 ± 73 pA) in primary motor neurons.
source: Notably, CoChR and ChrimsonR generated the largest photocurrents (CoChR 475 ± 186 pA, mean ± SD, N = 8 cells, ChrimsonR 251 ± 73 pA, N = 7; Figure 4E)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of photocurrent amplitudes with statistical descriptors, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Chronos showed the fastest deactivation kinetics (4.3 ± 0.4 ms) among cation channelrhodopsins.
source: Deactivation time constants were more variable between opsins, with Chronos showing the fastest deactivation kinetics (4.3 ± 0.4 ms, N = 3 cells, mean ± SD) and the other opsins displaying longer time constants (12–20 ms; Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of deactivation kinetics, supported by Figure 4G.

claim: CoChR and ChrimsonR were the only opsin lines capable of triggering spiking in primary motor neurons.
source: CoChR and ChrimsonR were the only opsin lines capable of triggering spiking in this cell type (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which opsins could induce spiking, supported by Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: 5 ms light pulses induced spikes in all CoChR-expressing neurons (N = 11 out of 11 cells at 3–30 mW/mm2).
source: Notably, 5 ms light pulses induced spikes in all CoChR-expressing neurons (N = 11 out of 11 cells at 3–30 mW/mm2)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on spike induction efficacy with exact cell counts.

claim: ChrimsonR could induce firing up to 100 Hz, with each light pulse typically evoking a single spike.
source: ChrimsonR could induce firing up to the highest frequency tested (100 Hz), with each light pulse typically evoking a single spike (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states ChrimsonR's capability for high-frequency firing, supported by Figure 5C,D.

claim: CoChR generated bursts of spikes in response to light pulses, even at the shortest stimulation duration.
source: CoChR generated bursts of spikes in response to light pulses, even at the shortest stimulation duration and spiking consistently attenuated in the second half of the stimulation train (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes CoChR's tendency to produce spike bursts, supported by Figure 5E,F.

claim: GtACRs achieved the strongest suppression of coil rate using blue light (90–95% decrease at 8.4–225 μW/mm2) in embryos.
source: GtACRs achieved the strongest suppression of coil rate using blue light (90–95% decrease at 8.4–225 μW/mm2; Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on behavioral suppression efficacy, supported by Figure 6F.

claim: With amber light, GtACR1, eArch3.0 and eNpHR3.0 showed comparable suppression (80–90% decrease at 50.5–227 μW/mm2) of embryonic coiling.
source: With amber light, GtACR1, eArch3.0 and eNpHR3.0 showed comparable suppression (80–90% decrease at 50.5–227 μW/mm2), with GtACR1 achieving ~83% decrease in coil rate even at low irradiance (15.9 μW/mm2; Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on behavioral suppression with amber light, supported by Figure 6G.

claim: Expression of GtACR1, GtACR2 and eArch3.0 in motor neurons and interneurons reduced swim bout rate relative to control larvae in response to blue light, with GtACRs achieving the greatest suppression (20–45% decrease).
source: Expression of GtACR1, GtACR2 and eArch3.0 in motor neurons and interneurons reduced swim bout rate relative to control larvae in response to blue light, with GtACRs achieving the greatest suppression (20–45% decrease; Figure 7D,E; Sternberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on larval swim suppression, supported by Figure 7D,E and a citation.

claim: Using red light, only eNpHR3.0 could reduce bout rate and suppression increased with higher irradiance (45% decrease at 1 mW/mm2).
source: Using red light, only eNpHR3.0 could reduce bout rate and suppression increased with higher irradiance (45% decrease at 1 mW/mm2; Figure 7F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on eNpHR3.0's efficacy with red light, supported by Figure 7F.

claim: GtACR1 photocurrents reversed with a positive 5–10 mV shift relative to ECl in both intracellular solutions tested.
source: Inspection of I-V curves for GtACR1 photocurrents showed that, in both solutions, currents reversed with a positive 5–10 mV shift relative to ECl (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B), as previously observed (Govorunova et al., 2015)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on GtACR1 reversal potential, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation.

claim: GtACRs induced photocurrents with peak amplitude 3–10 times larger than those generated by Cl–/H+ pumps.
source: GtACRs induced photocurrents with peak amplitude 3–10 times larger than those generated by Cl–/H+ pumps (Figure 8C)
evidence: The manuscript provides a comparative quantitative statement about photocurrent amplitudes, supported by Figure 8C.

claim: GtACR photocurrents had the fastest activation kinetics (~1 ms at 30 mW/mm2).
source: GtACR photocurrents had the fastest activation kinetics (~1 ms at 30 mW/mm2; Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on activation kinetics, supported by Figure 8E and supplementary figure.

claim: Deactivation kinetics of Cl–/H+ pumps were 2–10 times faster than those induced by GtACRs (14–22 ms eNpHR3.0, 27–37 ms eArch3.0).
source: However, deactivation kinetics of Cl–/H+ pumps were 2–10 times faster than those induced by GtACRs (14–22 ms eNpHR3.0, 27–37 ms eArch3.0; Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on deactivation kinetics with comparative analysis, supported by Figure 8G and supplementary figure.

claim: GtACRs and eNpHR3.0 could effectively inhibit spikes (80–95% suppression) in primary motor neurons.
source: We found that GtACRs and eNpHR3.0 could effectively inhibit spikes (80–95% suppression), while light pulses did not alter firing in opsin-negative neurons (Figure 9F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on spike inhibition efficacy, supported by Figure 9F.

claim: Both GtACR1 and eNpHR3.0 successfully inhibited tonic spiking during light pulses, with complete suppression in 60–100% of cells at 10 mW/mm2 irradiance.
source: Both GtACR1 and eNpHR3.0 successfully inhibited spiking during the light pulse, with complete suppression in 60–100% of cells at 10 mW/mm2 irradiance (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on tonic firing inhibition, supported by Figure 9G,H.

claim: Optogenetics has greatly advanced the ability to investigate how neural circuits process information and generate behaviour by allowing manipulation of neural activity with high spatio-temporal resolution.
source: Optogenetics has greatly advanced our ability to investigate how neural circuits process information and generate behaviour by allowing manipulation of neural activity with high spatio-temporal resolution in genetically-defined neurons (Miesenböck, 2009; Boyden, 2011; Miesenböck, 2011; Adamantidis et al., 2015; Boyden, 2015; Deisseroth, 2015; Deisseroth and Hegemann, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this established scientific consensus about optogenetics.

claim: Stable expression systems offer higher reliability and homogeneity than transient ones for optogenetic experiments.
source: reproducible opsin expression levels (across cells and animals), with stable expression systems offering higher reliability and homogeneity than transient ones (Kikuta and Kawakami, 2009; Yizhar et al., 2011; Sjulson et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this claim about the advantages of stable expression systems.

claim: The efficacy with which optogenetic actuators can control neuronal spiking in vivo depends on biophysical properties, expression level and membrane trafficking of the opsin, physiological properties of the target cell and the intensity profile of light delivered within scattering tissue.
source: The efficacy with which optogenetic actuators – such as microbial opsins – can control neuronal spiking in vivo depends on biophysical properties, expression level and membrane trafficking of the opsin, physiological properties of the target cell and the intensity profile of light delivered within scattering tissue.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established understanding based on scientific knowledge.

claim: Zebrafish offer genetic accessibility and transparency advantages for optogenetic studies.
source: In this study, we took advantage of the genetic accessibility and transparency of zebrafish (Arrenberg et al., 2009; Del Bene and Wyart, 2012; Arrenberg and Driever, 2013; Portugues et al., 2013; Förster et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support the advantages of zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: Optogenetic induction of few spikes in trigeminal neurons reliably elicits escape responses in zebrafish embryos.
source: In this class of somatosensory neuron, optogenetic induction of few spikes has been shown to reliably elicits escape responses (Douglass et al., 2008), characterised by high-amplitude bends of the trunk and tail (Kimmel et al., 1990; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998; Sagasti et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this established behavioral phenomenon.

claim: The excitatory effect of GtACRs suggests that increasing chloride conductance depolarises neurons at the embryonic developmental stage.
source: The excitatory effect of GtACRs suggests that increasing chloride conductance depolarises neurons at this developmental stage.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the observed excitatory effects of GtACRs in embryos.

claim: Some opsins showed higher response probability in transient transgenic animals (CheRiff, CoChR and GtACRs), likely due to higher expression levels.
source: Some opsins showed higher response probability in transient transgenic animals (CheRiff, CoChR and GtACRs), likely due to higher expression levels.
evidence: The manuscript infers that higher expression levels explain the difference in response probability between transient and stable transgenics.

claim: Longer tail movements observed in response to single light pulses indicate engagement of spinal central pattern generators.
source: However, longer movements (>100 ms, 4–5 cycles) were often observed in response to single light pulses (see response to 2 ms pulse in Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1) indicating engagement of spinal central pattern generators.
evidence: The manuscript infers the engagement of central pattern generators from the observed behavioral patterns.

claim: Engagement of spinal central pattern generators may occur through recruitment of glutamatergic V2a interneurons connected to motor neurons via gap junctions and/or by proprioceptive feedback via cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons.
source: This may occur through recruitment of glutamatergic V2a interneurons connected to motor neurons via gap junctions (Song et al., 2016) and/or by proprioceptive feedback via cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons (Wyart et al., 2009; Fidelin et al., 2015; Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about possible mechanisms based on cited literature.

claim: Opsin-expressing primary motor neurons displayed physiological properties, such as membrane resistance, resting membrane potential and cell capacitance, comparable to control opsin-negative cells.
source: Opsin-expressing pMNs displayed physiological properties, such as membrane resistance, resting membrane potential and cell capacitance, comparable to control opsin-negative cells (Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript provides data showing no significant differences in basic physiological properties between opsin-expressing and control cells.

claim: No significant irradiance-dependent modulation of photocurrent amplitude was observed in any cation channelrhodopsin line, likely due to the high range of irradiance tested.
source: We did not observe significant irradiance-dependent modulation of photocurrent amplitude in any opsin line, likely due to the high range of irradiance we tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript infers the reason for lack of irradiance dependence from the experimental conditions.

claim: Photocurrent kinetics influence the temporal precision with which single action potentials can be evoked.
source: Photocurrent kinetics influence the temporal precision with which single action potentials can be evoked (Mattis et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established principle.

claim: Primary motor neurons can spike at high frequency (up to 300–500 Hz).
source: Primary motor neurons can spike at high frequency (up to 300–500 Hz; Menelaou and McLean, 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this physiological property of primary motor neurons.

claim: Optogenetic induction of high-frequency firing should not be limited by cell intrinsic physiological properties, but rather by opsin properties and light stimulation parameters.
source: hence optogenetic induction of high-frequency firing should not be limited by cell intrinsic physiological properties, but rather by opsin properties and light stimulation parameters.
evidence: The manuscript infers this based on the known physiological capabilities of primary motor neurons.

claim: Spikes were induced with short latency (3–4 ms mean latency) and low jitter (0.25–1.25 ms jitter) with both CoChR and ChrimsonR lines.
source: Overall, spikes were induced with short latency (3–4 ms mean latency) and low jitter (0.25–1.25 ms jitter) with both opsin lines (Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on spike timing precision, supported by figures.

claim: Zebrafish embryos coil spontaneously between 24 and 27 hpf.
source: Embryos were tested between 24 and 27 hpf, a stage at which embryos coil spontaneously (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998)
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this developmental behavior.

claim: Zebrafish embryos show only minimal light-induced photomotor responses at 24-27 hpf, which mostly occur later in development (30–40 hpf).
source: but show only minimal light-induced photomotor responses, which mostly occur later in development (30–40 hpf) (Kokel et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this developmental timeline of photomotor responses.

claim: Light exposure led to a suppression of coiling behaviour that was followed by a synchronised restart at light offset in opsin-expressing embryos.
source: In opsin-expressing embryos, light exposure led to a suppression of coiling behaviour that was followed by a synchronised restart at light offset (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1; N = 91 ± 16 fish per group, mean ± SD), as previously reported (Warp et al., 2012; Mohamed et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript provides data on behavioral suppression and cites references to prior observations of this phenomenon.

claim: GtACR activation in spinal neurons occasionally induced movements in the initial 1–2 s following light onset.
source: As expected from behaviour with Tg(isl2b:GAL4) embryos (Figure 2F,G), GtACR activation in spinal neurons occasionally induced movements in the initial 1–2 s following light onset (black arrows in Figure 6D,E), a phenomenon that was not observed with Cl–/H+ pumps.
evidence: The manuscript describes observed behavioral patterns with reference to figures.

claim: Light decreased coiling in control opsin-negative embryos, yet to a significantly lesser degree than in opsin-expressing animals.
source: As previously observed (Friedmann et al., 2015), light also decreased coiling in control opsin-negative embryos, yet to a significantly lesser degree than in opsin-expressing animals (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: The manuscript provides comparative data and cites a reference to prior observations.

claim: Optogenetically evoked suppression of coiling was likely a result of distinct mechanisms in the different transgenic lines.
source: Optogenetically evoked suppression was likely a result of distinct mechanisms in the different transgenic lines.
evidence: The manuscript infers different mechanisms based on the different types of opsins used.

claim: Cl–/H+ pumps systematically induce hyperpolarisation.
source: While Cl–/H+ pumps systematically induce hyperpolarisation
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established property of these optogenetic tools.

claim: Anion channelrhodopsins can silence cells via shunting as well as depolarisation block depending upon the reversal potential of chloride in vivo.
source: anion channelrhodopsins can silence cells via shunting as well as depolarisation block depending upon the reversal potential of chloride in vivo (see below and Discussion).
evidence: The manuscript infers these mechanisms based on the properties of anion channelrhodopsins and chloride reversal potential.

claim: Opsin-negative larvae showed a 20–30% increase in bout rate during illumination with blue light.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Andalman et al., 2019), opsin-negative larvae showed a 20–30% increase in bout rate during illumination with blue light (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data and cites a reference to a prior observation.

claim: No increase in bout rate was found in larvae expressing anion channelrhodopsins even when analysis was restricted to the initial 2 s of the light period, suggesting GtACRs do not induce excitatory effects at larval stages.
source: No increase in bout rate was found in larvae expressing anion channelrhodopsins even when analysis was restricted to the initial 2 s of the light period (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), suggesting GtACRs do not induce excitatory effects at larval stages.
evidence: The manuscript infers the lack of excitatory effects from the behavioral data.

claim: Using the Tg(mnx1:GAL4) transgene to selectively drive expression only in motor neurons resulted in a decrease in bout speed (~20% reduction), but not bout rate.
source: By contrast, using the Tg(mnx1:GAL4) transgene to selectively drive expression only in motor neurons resulted in a decrease in bout speed (~20% reduction), but not bout rate (Figure 7—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the effects of motor neuron-specific opsin expression.

claim: Chloride reversal potential (ECl) is known to change over development.
source: Since anion channelrhodopsin function depends on chloride homeostasis (Figure 8A; Govorunova et al., 2015) and chloride reversal potential (ECl) is known to change over development (Ben-Ari, 2002; Reynolds et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this established developmental phenomenon.

claim: GtACR1 photocurrents were primarily driven by chloride ions.
source: This suggests that GtACR1 photocurrents were primarily driven by chloride ions, as expected (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the reversal potential data and cites a reference.

claim: Anion channelrhodopsins induced inward, 'depolarising' photocurrents while Cl–/H+ pumps generated outward, 'hyperpolarising' currents.
source: Anion channelrhodopsins induced inward, `depolarising` photocurrents (as expected from the combination of ECl and holding potential), while Cl–/H+ pumps generated outward, `hyperpolarising` currents (Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript provides data on photocurrent direction, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: All opsins except eNpHR3.0 showed bi-phasic photocurrent responses comprising a fast activation followed by a slow inactivation.
source: All opsins except eNpHR3.0 showed bi-phasic photocurrent responses comprising a fast activation followed by a slow inactivation (Figure 8B), likely due to a fraction of the opsin population transitioning to an inactive state (Chow et al., 2010; Mattis et al., 2011; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes observed photocurrent kinetics and cites references to explain the mechanism.

claim: Cl–/H+ pumps showed little inactivation (600–1000 ms eArch3.0).
source: and showed little inactivation (600–1000 ms eArch3.0; Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on inactivation kinetics, supported by figures.

claim: In a subset of GtACR1- (N = 4 out of 7) and GtACR2-expressing neurons (N = 2 out of 6), spiking was induced at light onset when using the ECl–50 mV solution.
source: In a subset of GtACR1- (N = 4 out of 7) and GtACR2-expressing neurons (N = 2 out of 6), spiking was induced at light onset when using the ECl–50 mV solution (Figure 9A; GtACR1 6.7 ± 7.1 spikes; GtACR2 1.5 ± 0.7, mean ± SD).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on spike induction with exact cell counts.

claim: The transient nature of spiking induced by GtACRs is consistent with the movements evoked at light onset in young, 1 dpf embryos expressing GtACRs.
source: This is consistent with the movements evoked at light onset in young, 1 dpf embryos expressing GtACRs (Figures 2 and 6).
evidence: The manuscript infers consistency between electrophysiological and behavioral observations.

claim: Data from eArch3.0-expressing neurons could not be collected due to degradation in the quality of recordings or cells becoming highly depolarised by the later stages of the protocol, suggesting that repeated eArch3.0 activation may alter electrical properties of neurons.
source: Data from eArch3.0-expressing neurons could not be collected due to degradation in the quality of recordings or cells becoming highly depolarised (i.e. resting membrane potential > –50 mV) by the later stages of the protocol, suggesting that repeated eArch3.0 activation may alter electrical properties of neurons (Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript infers potential effects of repeated activation from observed recording issues and cites a reference.

claim: GtACR1 could inhibit tonic spiking even when using the embryonic ECl–50 mV solution, consistent with the suppression of coiling behaviour upon prolonged illumination of GtACR-expressing embryos.
source: Notably, GtACR1 could inhibit tonic spiking even when using the embryonic ECl–50 mV solution (Figure 9G,H), consistent with the suppression of coiling behaviour upon prolonged illumination of GtACR-expressing embryos (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript infers consistency between electrophysiological and behavioral observations.

claim: High-throughput behavioural assays and whole-cell electrophysiological recordings provided complementary insights to guide tool selection.
source: High-throughput behavioural assays and whole-cell electrophysiological recordings provided complementary insights to guide tool selection (Figure 10).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the complementary nature of the two approaches.

claim: Behavioural assays enabled efficient evaluation of opsin lines in various sensory and motor cell types and revealed developmental stage-specific effects in intact neural populations.
source: Behavioural assays enabled efficient evaluation of opsin lines in various sensory and motor cell types and revealed developmental stage-specific effects in intact neural populations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the advantages of behavioral assays based on the study's findings.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings from single motor neurons afforded quantification of photocurrents and systematic evaluation of the ability of these optogenetic tools to elicit or silence activity at single action potential resolution.
source: Electrophysiological recordings from single motor neurons afforded quantification of photocurrents and systematic evaluation of the ability of these optogenetic tools to elicit or silence activity at single action potential resolution.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the advantages of electrophysiological recordings based on the study's findings.

claim: There was good qualitative agreement between behavioural and electrophysiological results, with efficacy in behavioural assays largely predicting rank order in photocurrent amplitudes.
source: Overall, there was good qualitative agreement between behavioural and electrophysiological results, with efficacy in behavioural assays (even with transient expression) largely predicting rank order in photocurrent amplitudes.
evidence: The manuscript infers this relationship from comparing the results of both approaches.

claim: This illustrates the utility of high-throughput behavioural assays for rapid evaluation and selection of expression constructs prior to more time-consuming generation and characterisation of stable lines and electrophysiological calibration.
source: This illustrates the utility of high-throughput behavioural assays for rapid evaluation and selection of expression constructs prior to more time-consuming generation and characterisation of stable lines and electrophysiological calibration.
evidence: The manuscript infers this practical implication from the study's findings.

claim: Broad variation in efficacy across lines was observed, likely attributable to differences in both the intrinsic properties of the opsin as well as variation in expression and membrane targeting.
source: We observed broad variation in efficacy across lines, likely attributable to differences in both the intrinsic properties of the opsin as well as variation in expression and membrane targeting.
evidence: The manuscript infers the causes of variation from the observed data.

claim: Membrane trafficking can be influenced by the fluorescent protein fused to the actuator.
source: Membrane trafficking can also be influenced by the fluorescent protein fused to the actuator (Arrenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this known effect.

claim: Better expression was observed with the tdTomato fusion than with previous attempts using a tagRFP fusion protein.
source: In our hands, we observed better expression with the tdTomato fusion reported here than with previous attempts using a tagRFP fusion protein.
evidence: The manuscript reports an empirical observation from the study.

claim: Expression might be further improved through codon optimisation, trafficking-enhancing sequences, alternative expression targeting systems and optimisation of the fluorescent reporter protein.
source: In the future, expression might be further improved through codon optimisation (Horstick et al., 2015), trafficking-enhancing sequences (Gradinaru et al., 2010; Mattis et al., 2011), alternative expression targeting systems (Luo et al., 2008; Sjulson et al., 2016) and optimisation of the fluorescent reporter protein.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about future improvements and cites references to support these possibilities.

claim: Although several opsin lines did not evoke action potentials in low-input-resistance pMNs, behavioural assays showed that all lines induced tail movements in larvae, likely due to recruitment of secondary motor neurons with higher input resistance.
source: Although several opsin lines did not evoke action potentials in low-input-resistance pMNs, behavioural assays showed that all lines induced tail movements in larvae. This is likely due to recruitment of secondary motor neurons labelled by the Tg(mnx1:GAL4) transgene, which have higher input resistance (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript infers this explanation from the discrepancy between electrophysiological and behavioral results, citing a reference.

claim: Behavioural assays at multiple ages revealed that anion channelrhodopsins can excite neurons in one dpf embryos which was corroborated by making whole-cell recordings using a patch solution reproducing the high intracellular chloride concentration observed in embryonic neurons.
source: Behavioural assays at multiple ages revealed that anion channelrhodopsins can excite neurons in one dpf embryos which was corroborated by making whole-cell recordings using a patch solution reproducing the high intracellular chloride concentration observed in embryonic neurons (Reynolds et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes how behavioral and electrophysiological findings corroborate each other, citing references.

claim: The platform enables efficient selection and calibration of optogenetic tools for in vivo neuroscience.
source: Overall, our platform enables efficient selection and calibration of optogenetic tools for in vivo neuroscience.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the utility of the developed platform.

claim: The platform enables opsin-specific optimisation of light delivery (i.e. wavelength, pulse duration, frequency and intensity).
source: It also enables opsin-specific optimisation of light delivery (i.e. wavelength, pulse duration, frequency and intensity).
evidence: The manuscript describes a capability of the platform.

claim: Equivalent stimulation regimes produced different rates of spiking adaptation that impacted the ability to control high-frequency firing, depending on the specific opsin line.
source: For example, we found that equivalent stimulation regimes produced different rates of spiking adaptation that impacted the ability to control high-frequency firing, depending on the specific ospin line in question.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observed differences in spiking patterns across opsin lines.

claim: Photocurrent amplitude, measured in pMNs, was proportional to estimated opsin expression level.
source: Photocurrent amplitude, measured in pMNs, was proportional to estimated opsin expression level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The manuscript describes a correlation observed in the data, supported by a figure.

claim: Photocurrent amplitude was predictive of the ability of opsin lines to induce behaviour via activation of distinct cell types at both larval and embryonic stages (CoChR > ChrimsonR > ChR2(H134R) > Chronos ≥ CheRiff).
source: and was predictive of the ability of opsin lines to induce behaviour via activation of distinct cell types at both larval and embryonic stages (CoChR > ChrimsonR > ChR2(H134R) > Chronos ≥ CheRiff).
evidence: The manuscript infers this predictive relationship from comparing photocurrent and behavioral data.

claim: CoChR evoked spikes in all pMNs tested and triggered behaviour with maximal response probability in larvae at irradiance levels as low as 0.63 mW/mm2.
source: Notably, CoChR evoked spikes in all pMNs tested and triggered behaviour with maximal response probability in larvae at irradiance levels as low as 0.63 mW/mm2.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on CoChR's efficacy.

claim: Light pulses can lead to bursts of spikes and substantial firing rate adaptation during high-frequency stimulation in primary motor neurons, likely a result of plateau potentials and inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: Our data indicate that in primary motor neurons, light pulses can lead to bursts of spikes and substantial firing rate adaptation during high-frequency stimulation, likely a result of plateau potentials and inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: The manuscript infers the mechanisms underlying observed spiking patterns.

claim: Although the CoChR line produced large-amplitude photocurrents and was highly efficient and precise in evoking the first spike, in primary motor neurons it was also prone to burst firing even for short (0.5 ms) light pulses, which compromised spiking entrainment with high-frequency stimulations.
source: Thus, although the CoChR line produced large-amplitude photocurrents and was highly efficient and precise in evoking the first spike, in this particular cell type it was also prone to burst firing even for short (0.5 ms) light pulses, which compromised spiking entrainment with high-frequency stimulations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes observed limitations of CoChR in this specific cell type.

claim: CoChR has been used to elicit single spikes in mouse pyramidal cells with 1 ms light pulses at frequencies up to 50 Hz.
source: However, CoChR has been used to elicit single spikes in mouse pyramidal cells with 1 ms light pulses at frequencies up to 50 Hz (Ronzitti et al., 2017).
